title: Rock Show

jokes.text: Your boobs are dead.
jokes.setup: Andy's casts are being removed at the hospital, a moment of relief and celebration.
jokes.punchline: Andy's first observation upon seeing his atrophied, withered legs is to call them 'dead boobs,' a weirdly childlike and absurd non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in character for Andy — childlike, inappropriate, and oddly specific. The economy is excellent (three words), and it lands because it's the last thing you'd expect someone to say about their own atrophied legs. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Congratulations, Andy. Your arms have healed perfectly. You can go back to normal activities.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's great! Hey, speaking of things that have healed, did you do something different? Because you are looking absolutely—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, no.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I was just going to say she has a nice... presence in the room.

jokes.text: Wow, it's like a sweaty piñata.
jokes.setup: Andy's casts are cracked open and removed, revealing the leg underneath.
jokes.punchline: Tom's reaction comparing the cast-opening to a sweaty piñata is unexpectedly vivid and grotesque.
jokes.explanation: The 'sweaty piñata' image is memorably gross and funny. Good economy, reasonably character-specific for Tom's style of commentary, and the simile is genuinely original.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Oh man, this is gonna feel so good. I can't wait to get this thing off.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Alright, let's get started.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Aaahhhhh! Oh my God! Oh my God, oh my God! It's like... it's like a thousand daggers made of ice are being driven into my skin! It's like a swarm of angry bees the size of birds! It's like I'm being attacked by a bear made of chainsaws!

jokes.text: Hey, my iPod! / Oh, yeah! My pirate!
jokes.setup: Objects have apparently been hidden inside Andy's cast for months.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from finding an iPod (plausible) to a pirate (absurd) inside the cast, each character delighted to find their lost item.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from realistic (iPod) to surreal ('my pirate') is a classic absurdist beat. The rewatch bonus is earned because on second viewing, the idea of a pirate being stored in a leg cast is funnier. The structure is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: How did a pirate get in my cast?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not a pirate, that's a peg leg.

jokes.text: This is a symbol of new beginnings, a symbol of hope, and of our project. We will build this park!
jokes.setup: Leslie holds a grotesque, months-old leg cast.
jokes.punchline: She delivers a soaring inspirational speech about the cast being a symbol of hope, completely unaware of the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely in the gap between Leslie's sincere grandeur and the disgusting object she's holding. Very high character integration — this is quintessential Leslie Knope behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It is gonna feel so good to walk again, finally.

jokes.text: Andy immediately falls when he tries to walk for the first time
jokes.setup: Andy has just gotten his casts off and is eager to walk again, saying 'It is gonna feel so good to walk again, finally.'
jokes.punchline: He immediately collapses. The reaction of horror from everyone ('Oh, no!') sells it.
jokes.explanation: Well-structured physical comedy — the setup line ('gonna feel so good to walk') is the perfect feed for the fall. Not the most original gag but well-timed with a good collective reaction beat.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: He's literally singing to a sandwich

jokes.text: He's been writing all these songs about things that are physically near him. / Sandwich! Are you turkey or ham? / Ham.
jokes.setup: Ann explains that being bedridden and bored drove Andy to songwriting.
jokes.punchline: The revealed song content — a sincere, rhyming rock song addressed to a nearby sandwich — is perfectly absurd. The sandwich 'answering' Ham makes it a complete mini-bit.
jokes.explanation: This is the funniest joke in the episode's first half. The setup (Ann's deadpan explanation) leads perfectly to the absurd song lyric, and the 'Ham.' response — delivered as though the sandwich answered — is an extra comedic flourish. High originality, perfect economy, quintessentially Andy. The structure of setup/explanation/song snippet/answer is airtight.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I want you to be a lamp. Just a lamp. That's all I'm asking.

jokes.text: Lamp! Wish you were a lamp that would light up when you get touched
jokes.setup: Ann has just revealed Andy writes songs about nearby objects, demonstrated with the sandwich song.
jokes.punchline: The lamp song continues the absurdist conceit and escalates it — the lamp song is even more poignantly ridiculous, a sincere desire for touch-sensitive lamp technology.
jokes.explanation: The lamp song is a callback/escalation of the sandwich bit and actually might be funnier on reflection — Andy singing sincerely to a lamp about wishing it were touch-activated is absurdism at its finest. The pathos of a lonely, immobilized man serenading household objects adds depth.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I don't like to define my music. It's just... you know, it's a fusion of rock, pop, a little bit of soul, some folk elements, and—

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: So it's rock.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I don't like to define my music.

jokes.text: What kind of music does your band play? / You know, I don't really like to define it, but it's like Matchbox Twenty meets The Fray. / So, rock. / Well, again, I don't really like to define it.
jokes.setup: Andy is invited to describe his band's genre.
jokes.punchline: His 'undefinable' music is immediately and correctly identified as just 'rock' by Leslie, and Andy still refuses to accept the label — a perfect puncturing of artistic pretension.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly structured two-beat joke: the pretentious artist reference (Matchbox Twenty + The Fray = extremely mainstream rock), the immediate deflating 'So, rock,' and Andy's continued refusal. The comedy comes from the gap between Andy's self-image and reality.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, I love mixing work and personal life. It's great. I do it all the time.

jokes.text: Oh, you guys. You know how I love mixing work into my personal life.
jokes.setup: Leslie is torn between going to Andy's concert and attending a political meeting her mom set up.
jokes.punchline: Her wry self-aware comment about loving to mix work into personal life, as she's literally choosing work over a fun social event.
jokes.explanation: A gentle self-deprecating character moment for Leslie. It's funny because it's true and she knows it, but it doesn't subvert expectations much — it confirms what we already know about her. Solid but not standout.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I lowered a speed bump by two inches. That's what government does.

jokes.text: Mark's speed bump achievement: 'I got it lowered 2 inches. Apparently what I can achieve in government can literally be measured.'
jokes.setup: Mark is congratulated on getting the speed bump 'thing' taken care of — sounds like a genuine accomplishment
jokes.punchline: The achievement was lowering a speed bump by 2 inches — and Mark's rueful self-awareness that this is the literal measurable limit of his impact
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The deadpan double meaning of 'literally measured' — the bureaucratic achievement is physically a measurement of inches — is genuinely clever. Strong character integration: Mark's weary cynicism about government is perfectly distilled. Very quotable as a line about institutional futility.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: He wrote a song about the pit. It's called 'The Pit' and it's just him rocking out while singing about how dangerous it is and listing all the municipal codes that were violated.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It's somehow both the hardest rocking song I've ever heard and the most informative.

jokes.text: There used to be this huge speed bump in the center of town. It was insane. So, I decided I wanted to do something about it, and I got it lowered 2 inches. Apparently, what I can achieve in government can literally be measured.
jokes.setup: Mark is congratulated for getting the speed bump issue resolved.
jokes.punchline: His talking-head reveals the enormous effort it took to accomplish something that can be measured in inches — a perfect encapsulation of government bureaucracy's futility, delivered with deadpan resignation.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The line 'what I can achieve in government can literally be measured' is excellent — it works on multiple levels (the literal inches, the metaphorical smallness of achievement). Perfect deadpan delivery implied, strong originality, highly quotable. Captures the show's satirical core efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We could be The Sweetums, or The Pit Crew, or Mouse Rat, or The Doppelgangers, or Everything Rhymes with Orange, or The Bipeds, or Scarecrow Boat, or Urfascism, or The Slugs, or DJ Roomba and the Carpet Cleaners, or The Andy Bernard Experience, or Kielbasa Factory, or Boyz II Menorah, or The Decibels, or Punch Face Champions, or Fiscal Responsibility, or Ninja Shoe Repair, or The Possum Pendulum, or Kidney Stone, or Puppy Attack, or The Schnozberries, or The Blahs, or The Ew's, or Electric Nose Hair Trimmer, or Beets by Schrute, or...and honestly, we're never going to make it as a band because we waste all our time coming up with band names.

jokes.text: He wrote this new song about what happened to him called The Pit. It's one of those rare songs that rocks really hard, and also informs people about a small public works project.
jokes.setup: Ann is promoting Andy's concert and talking up his new material.
jokes.punchline: The sincere description of a rock song that 'informs people about a small public works project' is a perfect absurd collision of two incompatible registers.
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'rocks really hard, and also informs people about a small public works project' is a wonderfully deadpan formulation that encapsulates the show's central absurdity. Ann delivering it straight makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: George
dialogue.line: The divorce was really tough on the kids.

dialogue.speaker: George
dialogue.line: My adult children's kids. My own kids are doing great.

jokes.text: I have waited on him hand and foot for two months. / Well, I guess that explains it.
jokes.setup: The doctor reveals Andy's casts were supposed to come off two weeks ago and he chose to reschedule for unexplained personal reasons.
jokes.punchline: Ann's outraged declaration that she's been waiting on him 'hand and foot' is immediately recontextualized — Andy deliberately extended his recovery to keep being waited on. The doctor's dry 'Well, I guess that explains it' is the perfect button.
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully constructed reveal. The setup builds across the scene as the doctor reveals the truth, and Ann's idiom 'hand and foot' lands with full dramatic irony — the audience realizes Andy faked his recovery to keep Ann serving him. The doctor's understated button is perfection. Strong rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: George
dialogue.line: Leslie is like Sandy Duncan.

dialogue.speaker: George
dialogue.line: You know, that actress from the seventies.

jokes.text: The band name list: Teddy Bear Suicide, Mouse Rat, God Hates Figs, Department of Homeland Obscurity, Flames for Flames, Muscle Confusion, Nothing Rhymes with Orange, Everything Rhymes with Orange, Punch Face Champions, Rad Wagon, Puppy Pendulum, Possum Pendulum, Penis Pendulum, Hand Rail Suicide, Angel Snack, Just the Tip, Three Skin, Jet Black Pope...
jokes.setup: Andy introduces Scarecrow Boat at the concert and mentions the band has had a few different names.
jokes.punchline: The list of band names escalates from merely stupid to brilliantly absurd (Nothing/Everything Rhymes with Orange, the Pendulum trilogy, Just the Tip, Three Skin) before ending with Jet Black Pope. The sheer volume and internal logic variations are the joke.
jokes.explanation: This is the comedic highlight of the episode and one of Parks and Recreation's most beloved running jokes in embryo. The list works on multiple levels: the internal logic (Nothing/Everything Rhymes with Orange is a perfect pair), the escalating darkness (Teddy Bear Suicide, Hand Rail Suicide), the pendulum family (Puppy → Possum → Penis is a masterclass in escalation), and the bathos of ending on 'Jet Black Pope' before returning to Mouse Rat. Each name is individually funny and the cumulative effect is enormous. Very high originality and character integration — this couldn't come from any other show or character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie's Mom
dialogue.line: Honey, you need to give this date a real chance. Just finish dinner, have a nice conversation. And then have sex with him.

jokes.text: God, when I hear myself say Scarecrow Boat out loud, I kind of hate it.
jokes.setup: Andy has just delivered the enormous list of band names, culminating in the current name Scarecrow Boat.
jokes.punchline: Andy's immediate self-critique of the name he just introduced himself with, mid-performance, is a perfect moment of unfiltered self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the enormous list is beautifully self-aware. After cataloguing all those names, Andy's decision to hate the current one on the spot is very funny. It plants the seed for the later callback where he abandons 'Scarecrow Boat' entirely.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm revenge dating my ex-wife's sister. It's like a fairy tale.

jokes.text: Leslie's 'date' is actually a political meeting her mother set up, revealed gradually as Leslie pivots from zoning codes to the man discussing her dating life
jokes.setup: Leslie arrives at what she believes is a political 'tête-à-tête' and launches into zoning code questions.
jokes.punchline: The man begins commenting on her dating life, revealing this is actually a blind date her mother arranged under false pretenses.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed slow-burn reveal. The audience catches on slightly before Leslie does (when he mentions 'most women I go out with'), making the eventual recognition satisfying. Good structural misdirection.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I want you all to meet my wife, Wendy. She's incredibly attractive and she makes a lot of money.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: Tom, we've talked about this.

jokes.text: Leslie's 'date' asks 'What kind of movies do you like?' mid-political-discussion, shifting the entire dynamic
jokes.setup: Leslie is deep in a policy discussion about zoning codes and park development
jokes.punchline: George pivots to a date question — the audience (and Leslie) realize something is off
jokes.explanation: The joke is more of a slow burn setup than a standalone punchline — it plants the seed that this isn't a political meeting. Functional cringe comedy setup. The payoff is the reveal that it's a blind date.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Derek is a very serious person. He doesn't do anything fun or silly. He's all business.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We made out behind the Sweetums factory when we were both drunk.

jokes.text: It's refreshing to be with someone who actually likes talking about government issues. Most of the women I go out with find it boring.
jokes.setup: Leslie is happily discussing zoning codes, thinking she's at a work meeting.
jokes.punchline: His comment about 'women I go out with' is the first clear signal this is a date, creating dramatic irony as the audience realizes before Leslie does.
jokes.explanation: A functional misdirection beat that advances the blind date reveal. Not particularly original on its own but serves the larger joke well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm a seventh wheel.

jokes.text: It hasn't been easy. And I'm coping, but it was tough on the kids. Not my kids, 'cause they're grown-up, but it was tough on their kids. Shouldn't bring up my divorce on a first date.
jokes.setup: George mentions his divorce casually.
jokes.punchline: The escalation — it was tough on the kids → not his kids (they're grown) → tough on the grandkids — followed by the self-aware 'shouldn't bring up my divorce on a first date' fully confirms this is a date and reveals how old George is.
jokes.explanation: The loop of 'kids → grown-up kids → their kids' efficiently conveys that George is in his 60s while also being funny in its own right. The self-aware button ('shouldn't bring up my divorce') is a nice cringe comedy beat.

jokes.text: I think it's going quite well. And she looks like a young Sandy Duncan.
jokes.setup: We cut to George's talking head — implying a confessional — after the increasingly awkward date.
jokes.punchline: His completely sincere positivity about the date, and specifically the Sandy Duncan comparison (a reference that reveals his age), is a perfect character comedy moment.
jokes.explanation: The Sandy Duncan comparison is perfectly chosen — age-specific enough to be funny without being a mere name-drop, and 'young Sandy Duncan' applied to a contemporary woman is wonderfully oblivious. The contrast with how the date is actually going adds irony.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey Ann, can you get me a drink?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Sure, what do you want?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'll have a triple shot of vodka, a double shot of rum, and a splash of water.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's mostly alcohol!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, that's why I asked for the water. I'm trying to stay hydrated.

jokes.text: Hi, Mom. He thinks we're on a date. / Did you tell him we were on a date? / Honey, if I told you it was a date, you never would've gone. / You're not getting any younger. / Well, neither is he. And he's 62 years old.
jokes.setup: Leslie excuses herself to call her mom, having realized this is a blind date.
jokes.punchline: Her mother's complete lack of remorse and the logic of 'you never would've gone' — confirmed correct — followed by Leslie's rebuttal 'well, neither is he, and he's 62' perfectly captures their relationship dynamic.
jokes.explanation: The mother-daughter dynamic is efficiently established in a few lines. The implication that tricking Leslie was the only viable strategy is a nice character reveal, and Leslie's indignant 'well, neither is he' comeback is sharp.

dialogue.speaker: George
dialogue.line: The Everly Brothers are not remotely rock music

jokes.text: You don't have to have sex with him if you don't want to.
jokes.setup: Leslie's mother is trying to talk her into staying on the blind date.
jokes.punchline: The casually offered reassurance that sex is optional — implying it was at least on the table as a possibility — is a perfect shocking button to the phone call.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly timed and perfectly understated. The fact that her mother even frames it this way reveals a lot about their relationship dynamic while being genuinely shocking. Excellent economy — the shorter the line, the funnier it is.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: This next song is dedicated to my girlfriend. It's called 'April.' April, April, April, April, April, April, April, April, April, April, April, April...

jokes.text: Mark introduces his date: 'This is Beth, my ex-wife Tammy's better-looking sister.'
jokes.setup: Mark introduces his new date to the group
jokes.punchline: He defines her entirely through her relationship to his ex-wife and the comparative attractiveness judgment — casually brutal
jokes.explanation: The total absence of social grace in calling her the 'better-looking sister' as if that's a neutral descriptive fact is Mark in a nutshell. Economical and specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What about 'The Procrastinators'? Oh wait, you haven't decided yet.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Or 'Andy and the No-Shows' - because that's what you do to me.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: 'The Unreliables'? 'Flaky and the Disappointed'? 'Ann Deserves Better: A Musical Journey'?

jokes.text: This is Beth, my ex-wife Tammy's better-looking sister.
jokes.setup: Mark introduces his new date to the group.
jokes.punchline: The casual, completely unfiltered introduction that openly ranks his date above his ex-wife — as an introduction, to her face — is wonderfully inappropriate.
jokes.explanation: The economy of this introduction is its strength — all the weird backstory compressed into a single sentence. Mark's complete comfort saying this speaks to his character.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I'm not hitting on you.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: But would you be interested in getting dinner sometime?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: My ex-wife Tammy cheated on me. Then we divorced. Then last week, I ran into her sister Beth here. Turns out she hates Tammy, too, so we've started dating. It's like a fairy tale. / Yeah, Tammy stinks.
jokes.setup: Mark explains how he and Beth got together.
jokes.punchline: 'It's like a fairy tale' applied to a relationship built on mutual hatred of a third party, confirmed by Beth's cheerfully agreeable 'Yeah, Tammy stinks.'
jokes.explanation: The 'fairy tale' framing is the key subversion, and Beth's enthusiastic 'Tammy stinks' is a perfect button. The joke efficiently introduces a new character while being genuinely funny.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I fell in the pit. I fell in the pit. I fell in the pit.

jokes.text: Look at how hot she is. Isn't that crazy? And she's a surgeon. She makes a ton of money! Bam!
jokes.setup: Tom introduces his wife Wendy to Mark.
jokes.punchline: Tom's introduction is entirely about showing off, culminating in 'Bam!' — revealing his insecurity and the transactional nature of his pride in his wife.
jokes.explanation: Very strong character integration — the escalating bragging ('hot... surgeon... ton of money... BAM!') is pure Tom Haverford. The 'Bam!' as a punctuation mark is perfectly him.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The band is now officially called... Scarecrow Boat!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, no. Mouse Rat. We're Mouse Rat.

jokes.text: This is Derek. / Cool. How long have you guys been dating? / We're just friends. / He's like the gayest person I've ever met. But I make out with him when I'm drunk sometimes.
jokes.setup: Tom introduces his apparent friend Derek.
jokes.punchline: Tom's casual description of Derek ('gayest person I've ever met') followed by the complete non-sequitur that he makes out with him when drunk is delivered as though it perfectly explains the situation.
jokes.explanation: The logic gap — 'he's the gayest person I've ever met' → 'but I make out with him when drunk' — is funny precisely because Tom delivers it as if these facts are in harmony. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Do you know Todd from Indiana State?

dialogue.speaker: George
dialogue.line: I don't think so. What year did he graduate?

dialogue.speaker: George
dialogue.line: Oh no, I graduated in 2013. That's a 37-year gap.

jokes.text: You know, if you don't wanna talk to me, you can just say so. / I don't wanna talk to you.
jokes.setup: Mark has been on the receiving end of Tom's increasingly bizarre introductions.
jokes.punchline: Mark gives Tom the 'polite' out and Tom immediately takes the literal version of it without hesitation.
jokes.explanation: A clean setup/punchline with excellent economy. Mark sets up the social nicety and Tom immediately weaponizes the literal interpretation. Very Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Is he dead?

jokes.text: Apparently, tonight, I'm the Parks Department's seventh wheel.
jokes.setup: Mark surveys the scene: couples, a gay friend, a wife — everyone is paired off in increasingly unusual configurations.
jokes.punchline: 'Seventh wheel' instead of 'third wheel' perfectly quantifies just how alone and how complicated the social situation is.
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — the upgrade from 'third wheel' to 'seventh wheel' does a lot of work in three words, implicitly characterizing all the bizarre pairings at the concert. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie's boyfriend has Benjamin Button disease. He's getting younger every day. Soon he'll be a baby, then a fetus, then just a gleam in his father's eye.

jokes.text: George bringing his two grown sons on Leslie's blind date — as a family activity
jokes.setup: Leslie arrives back at the dinner table
jokes.punchline: George has his adult sons present at the table, introducing them on what is supposed to be a first date
jokes.explanation: Strong escalation of the blind date cringe — bringing your grown sons to meet a date is a level of social obliviousness that perfectly compounds the age-gap absurdity already established.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Yeah, Leslie dates older guys. Pretty soon she'll be one of those people on the Today Show where Al Roker's like, 'Margaret, you're 103 years old, what's your secret?' And Margaret's like, 'I've been dating Leslie Knope.'

jokes.text: Chicken, chicken, chicken! / Mmm. / Delicious, right? / Mmm-hmm. / I really like this restaurant. / Yeah. It's a great place for a business meeting.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to reframe the dinner as a business meeting after realizing it's a date.
jokes.punchline: George force-feeds Leslie chicken with escalating enthusiasm ('chicken, chicken, chicken!'), and Leslie's final deadpan insistence that this is 'a great place for a business meeting' while being literally hand-fed is the cringe payoff.
jokes.explanation: The 'chicken, chicken, chicken!' escalation is genuinely funny and the cringe of Leslie being force-fed while calling it a business meeting is well-executed. George's oblivious enthusiasm sells the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The only similarities are bar and drunk Mark.

jokes.text: George and his son force-feeding Leslie chicken: 'Chicken, chicken, chicken!'
jokes.setup: George offers Leslie a taste of his chicken; she declines
jokes.punchline: The pressure escalates into a chant of 'Chicken, chicken, chicken!' — crossing from awkward insistence to absurd peer pressure
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'chicken, chicken, chicken' takes a social cringe moment and pushes it into absurdism through sheer persistence. Funny in how it escalates from polite offer to bizarre chant.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: We could just throw our trash in the pit.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What?! No! That's where we're building the park!

jokes.text: Babe, hey. We're just about to start. Could you grab me a triple whiskey water? / You would like that, wouldn't you? / Yep. / You have two perfectly good legs. Get it yourself.
jokes.setup: Ann has just learned Andy faked needing the casts for two more weeks; now Andy casually asks her to fetch his drink.
jokes.punchline: Ann's devastating 'You have two perfectly good legs. Get it yourself' is the perfect, earned callback to the revelation that Andy's legs were fine — it's both a joke and a character turning point.
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's best jokes. The setup is the entire scene at the doctor's office, and the payoff is perfectly calibrated — Ann's response is both the punchline and a character beat, using the exact logic of the revelation ('two perfectly good legs') as a weapon. Earned, character-specific, quotable, and structurally tight.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Despite the pit's size, she completely missed it

jokes.text: The band is now called Scarecrow Boat at the show — having not changed back to Mouse Rat yet
jokes.setup: Andy introduced the band as Scarecrow Boat and immediately said he hated the name
jokes.punchline: He introduces them as Scarecrow Boat at the show anyway, having apparently not resolved his own crisis
jokes.explanation: Mild callback joke — it pays off the earlier self-awareness gag. Not a huge laugh but consistent character work.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. I'll admit it. I kind of enjoyed having everyone wait on me hand and foot.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Andy, you said your casts were medically necessary!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: They were! Mostly. But yeah, the whole being pampered thing? That was pretty great.

jokes.text: You already asked me that. / Oh. Sorry. Senior moment.
jokes.setup: The date/meeting has been awkward, and George asks Leslie the same movie question he asked earlier.
jokes.punchline: George's casual self-diagnosis of 'senior moment' is funny both as self-deprecating humor and as an inadvertent confirmation of the age gap Leslie is now keenly aware of.
jokes.explanation: A functional callback joke that builds on the awkwardness of the date. Not particularly original but serves the scene's cringe comedy well.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Well, it's already a park. We've got a pit, kids can play in it, slide down, break their arms. It's great.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: We could do duck-duck-goose, except the goose is a rabid German Shepherd.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Red Rover, but instead of a rope, it's barbed wire.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Simon Says, but if you don't do it perfectly, you get shocked with a cattle prod.

jokes.text: The last rock show I went to was the Everly Brothers.
jokes.setup: George enthusiastically agrees to go to the rock show, saying he hasn't been to one in a long time.
jokes.punchline: His last rock show being the Everly Brothers establishes both his age and his complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: A simple but effective age joke. The Everly Brothers reference is specific enough to be genuinely funny rather than generic, and his sincerity about it elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: You know what? Building this park is just like the moon landing. It seems impossible, everyone says you can't do it, but then you do it anyway and it's beautiful and everyone cries.

jokes.text: I am getting very positive signals.
jokes.setup: Leslie is being polite about his suggestion to go to the rock show, which he interprets as romantic interest.
jokes.punchline: His completely delusional interpretation of basic social courtesy as 'very positive signals' is a perfect oblivious character moment.
jokes.explanation: George's obliviousness is consistent and funny. The formal phrasing 'very positive signals' adds to the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't want this to happen again.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Again?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I mean... I don't want this to happen.

jokes.text: Hey, the band's really good. I liked that song Grapple Hound. / Gossip Town? / Right.
jokes.setup: George is chatting about the band at the venue.
jokes.punchline: George misremembers the song title so badly ('Grapple Hound' for 'Gossip Town') that it barely sounds like the same words, and Ann's patient correction — followed by his breezy 'Right' — is perfect.
jokes.explanation: The specific wrongness of 'Grapple Hound' for 'Gossip Town' is better than a generic misremembering — the words don't sound alike at all, which makes it funnier. George's unperturbed 'Right' sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: A park? In Pawnee? That pit's been there for years. Nothing's ever gonna change that.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I'm telling you, this is a waste of time and money.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Whoa!

jokes.text: Yeah, they should change their name to Big, Lying Baby. Or Where's My Sandwich? Or Don't Forget To Bring Home Beers After Work.
jokes.setup: George criticizes the band name, and Ann agrees they should change it.
jokes.punchline: Ann's suggested band names are all passive-aggressive jabs at Andy's laziness and the specific lies that Ann has recently discovered, delivered as though she's just brainstorming.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's finest jokes. Each suggested band name is a perfectly formed passive-aggressive accusation disguised as creative brainstorming. 'Big, Lying Baby' (Andy lied about his recovery), 'Where's My Sandwich?' (a callback to both the sandwich song and the food-fetching), 'Don't Forget To Bring Home Beers After Work' (the specificity of this one implies a long history). Exceptional character integration — this could only be Ann in this specific moment. Highly quotable and earns its impact through accumulated story context.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Andy's song plays as the credits roll, now literally true for Mark too

jokes.text: I don't get you and... I mean, it doesn't make any sense to me. I mean, I like Andy a lot. But there's tons of guys out there who have jobs and who respect you and think you're attractive. / Really? / Oh, yeah.
jokes.setup: Mark is gently trying to point out that Ann can do better than Andy.
jokes.punchline: Ann's genuinely surprised 'Really?' at the idea that other men find her attractive inadvertently reveals how much Andy has eroded her self-confidence.
jokes.explanation: A well-observed character beat that's both funny and slightly poignant. Ann's 'Really?' lands as a laugh but also shows the damage Andy has done to her confidence.

jokes.text: You mean guys like you... / No! / For instance? / No, no, no, no, no, not me.
jokes.setup: Mark is claiming there are better guys for Ann, implying he's not one of them.
jokes.punchline: Ann immediately and correctly reads his subtext, and Mark's panicked denial ('No! No, no, no, no, no, not me') is funny precisely because it's so emphatic.
jokes.explanation: A functional cringe comedy exchange. The back-and-forth is well-paced and Mark's increasingly desperate denial is funny because it protests too much.

jokes.text: Oh. Okay. Good, 'cause, for a second there, I thought you were hitting on me in front of my boyfriend. / No! Not my style. / Even though you did just call him a big, lying baby. And I do find you attractive.
jokes.setup: Mark has been insisting he's not hitting on Ann.
jokes.punchline: Ann uses Mark's own words against him — pointing out he both insulted her boyfriend and admitted she's attractive, which is the literal definition of what he claims he's not doing.
jokes.explanation: Ann's logical trap is well-constructed — she's right, and Mark can't deny it. The callback to 'big, lying baby' gives the line extra punch.

jokes.text: But if I were, would you be interested? / No. / Okay. / Let me tell you why, because I'm in a crappy mood...
jokes.setup: Mark has been protesting he's not hitting on Ann.
jokes.punchline: Mark's 'but if I were, would you be interested?' is a perfect example of deniable flirtation — the ask hidden inside a hypothetical — and Ann's flat 'No.' followed by an extended list of reasons is funnier than a simple rejection.
jokes.explanation: The 'hypothetical' flirtation is a classic comedic maneuver and it's well executed here. Ann's immediate and unambiguous 'No' is the first laugh, and her willingness to explain at length is the second.

jokes.text: Pit! I fell in it, the pit / You fell in it, the pit / We all fell in it, the pit
jokes.setup: The band plays its song 'The Pit' — Ann's description was that it 'rocks really hard and also informs people about a small public works project.'
jokes.punchline: The song is revealed to be exactly as described: extremely simple, repetitive lyrics that do nothing but describe the pit from different perspectives, delivered with full rock conviction.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Ann's earlier description is near-perfect. The song's structure — first person, second person, third person, all about falling in the pit — is both minimalist and perfectly logical for Andy's character. The commitment to the bit (it's a full song with a chorus) makes it funnier. The song also pays off later when Mark actually falls in the pit.

jokes.text: Thank you very much, everybody! We are Scarecrow Boat! No! Screw it! We are Mouse Rat! Thank you very much! Good night!
jokes.setup: Andy hated the name Scarecrow Boat when he said it earlier; now he's closing the show.
jokes.punchline: Mid-signoff, Andy abandons the name he's been performing under all night and reverses back to Mouse Rat in a single impulsive moment, treating the band name like an afterthought.
jokes.explanation: The callback payoff to both the band name list and Andy's self-criticism of 'Scarecrow Boat' is extremely well-earned. The impulsive 'Screw it!' mid-sentence captures Andy's character perfectly. This also sets up the show's running gag of Mouse Rat being their 'real' name.

jokes.text: Damn it. I missed it?
jokes.setup: Leslie arrives at the venue immediately after the band finishes.
jokes.punchline: Her devastated 'Damn it. I missed it?' is a perfect beat — her entire evening was spent trying to get here, and she arrived thirty seconds too late.
jokes.explanation: A well-timed reaction beat that pays off Leslie's subplot. The timing is the joke — she arrives the moment it ends.

jokes.text: Hi. I'm Tom Haverford. This is my wife, Wendy. She's my age.
jokes.setup: Tom introduces himself and Wendy to Leslie's elderly date George.
jokes.punchline: The completely unnecessary clarification 'She's my age' reveals Tom is self-conscious about the age dynamics in the room (George is much older), and his need to establish this immediately is a perfect character beat.
jokes.explanation: The unprompted, defensive 'She's my age' in an introduction is a perfect character reveal for Tom. It implies awareness of how absurd the group dynamic is and Tom's need to differentiate himself from the old man.

jokes.text: I have no idea why Ann is upset with me. But I do know she's too nice to yell at me in front of all these people. So, I am not leaving this bar.
jokes.setup: Andy has just been confronted by Ann and told to get his own drink.
jokes.punchline: Andy's talking-head reveals he knows exactly why Ann is upset but has consciously calculated that her niceness is a shield protecting him from consequences — so he's weaponizing her kindness.
jokes.explanation: This is a brilliant character comedy moment that reframes Andy from oblivious to strategically oblivious. The logic — she's too nice to yell at me in public, therefore I won't give her a private opportunity — is perfectly Andy and reveals a strategic intelligence beneath his apparent stupidity. Highly quotable and character-specific.

jokes.text: So, did you go to Indiana State? / Yes. / My buddy Todd went there. Maybe you know him. What year did you graduate? / 1968. / Oh! Todd graduated in 2005, so you probably missed him.
jokes.setup: Tom is making small talk with George, Leslie's elderly date.
jokes.punchline: Tom casually asks if George knows his friend Todd, then upon learning the 37-year gap in graduation dates, delivers 'you probably missed him' as if the math just slightly didn't work out.
jokes.explanation: The joke hinges on Tom treating a 37-year gap as a minor timing issue ('you probably missed him') — the understatement applied to a gap of decades is the joke. Well-structured, economy is excellent, and 'you probably missed him' is highly quotable.

jokes.text: I think I should head home now. / Okay. / It was nice to meet you. / It was fun. / I had a nice time. Don't think I'll go out with her again. / There was just no spark.
jokes.setup: George and Leslie say their polite goodbyes after the disastrous date.
jokes.punchline: George's talking-head reveal that he found no spark with Leslie — reversing the expected dynamic where the younger person rejects the older one — is a perfect reversal.
jokes.explanation: The reversal — George rejecting Leslie rather than the expected reverse — is a strong comedic choice. His casual 'no spark' as though this were a normal date between equals is the key absurdist touch.

jokes.text: How did Leslie meet her boyfriend? / She used to read him books at the senior center. / Wow. How old is he? / He's six, but he has Benjamin Button's disease.
jokes.setup: Someone asks about Leslie's dating history.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that she reads books to the senior center is misdirection toward George being older; 'he's six, but he has Benjamin Button's disease' is an absurdist escalation that pays off the misdirection unexpectedly.
jokes.explanation: This is a tightly constructed misdirection joke. The setup builds toward one assumption (old man at a senior center) and the punchline inverts it entirely (six-year-old with aging disease). The specificity of 'Benjamin Button's disease' rather than just 'a disease' is what elevates it. Strong structure and originality.

jokes.text: Hey, who wants to see me climb a tree? / I do! / I do!
jokes.setup: Andy's legs have just been established as fully functional, but he's been using his disability as leverage.
jokes.punchline: Andy's immediate pivot to showing off his recovered legs by climbing a tree — childlike, performative, and completely deflating the romantic drama — is a perfect character beat.
jokes.explanation: Andy's solution to awkward interpersonal tension is to literally climb a tree and get enthusiastic volunteers — a very character-specific way to break a dramatic moment. The enthusiasm of the 'I do!' responses makes it funnier.

jokes.text: You know what? That guy was too young for you. You should be dating guys in their early hundreds. I'm telling you, you should be dating men that Al Roker announces their birthdays.
jokes.setup: Leslie is upset about being set up with a 62-year-old (or possibly older) man.
jokes.punchline: Mark's 'comfort' by suggesting she should date men even older — men in their 'early hundreds,' men old enough to get a Today Show birthday shoutout from Al Roker — is a perfectly calibrated escalation.
jokes.explanation: The Al Roker birthday announcement reference is extremely specific and exactly the right level of cultural specificity — everyone knows this Today Show tradition and it perfectly captures being so old it's newsworthy. 'Early hundreds' is a wonderful construction. This is genuinely strong joke writing.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah. I made a bump into a smaller bump. It's a great day for America.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to make Mark feel better about his speed bump achievement by pointing out it fixed a real problem.
jokes.punchline: Mark's completely deflated 'I made a bump into a smaller bump. It's a great day for America' is a perfect deadpan that simultaneously mocks his achievement and the entire enterprise of local government.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the speed bump subplot is very strong here. 'I made a bump into a smaller bump' is the perfect self-summary of his achievement, and appending 'It's a great day for America' with complete deadpan extends the joke through ironic patriotic grandeur. Highly quotable. The economy (17 words) is excellent.

jokes.text: Mark and I are really connecting tonight. Like we connected that night when we made love five years ago. There's actually a lot of similarities between those two nights. That time we were also at a bar. And he was also pretty drunk.
jokes.setup: Leslie is sharing a nice moment with Mark over drinks.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's talking-head draws a parallel to their previous hookup, then the 'similarities' she identifies are 'also at a bar' and 'he was also pretty drunk' — implying the original encounter was not exactly a meeting of equals.
jokes.explanation: This is a masterfully constructed talking-head joke. The setup is warm (Leslie connecting with Mark), the pivot to 'like when we made love' is the first subversion, and then the 'similarities' she lists — bar, drunk — retroactively characterize the original hookup as less romantic than Leslie remembers. The structure is near-perfect: each beat lands, and the implication darkens without Leslie realizing it. Strong character integration and originality.

jokes.text: "But then you'd be homeless." — Mark's response to Leslie saying she'd live in the park
jokes.setup: Leslie rhapsodizes about the park design: 'God, that sounds wonderful. I would live in that park.'
jokes.punchline: Mark immediately and literally points out the logical consequence
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient deadpan — the literalism undercuts Leslie's enthusiasm in a gentle way. Good economy but not a particularly novel joke type.

jokes.text: Damn it! I was so close there! / Yeah, so... It was pretty close! / So far to the left! So far to the left!
jokes.setup: Mark has thrown a beer bottle attempting to land it in the pit and missed.
jokes.punchline: Both Mark and Leslie commentate on the missed shot with sports-announcer energy — their shared enthusiasm for a completely trivial and mildly illegal act is a bonding moment played as physical comedy.
jokes.explanation: A fun physical comedy beat that shows Leslie loosening up. The mutual enthusiasm about a failed bottle-toss is charming but not particularly sophisticated comedy.

jokes.text: Unbelievable! That's unbelievable! / You missed the entire pit, which is huge, by the way.
jokes.setup: Leslie has thrown her bottle at the pit.
jokes.punchline: She missed the entire pit — which, as Mark notes, is huge. The escalation of incompetence (Mark at least got close; Leslie missed completely) is funny.
jokes.explanation: A functional physical comedy beat. 'Which is huge, by the way' is a good addition that highlights the absurdity of missing such a large target.

jokes.text: I waited on you hand and foot. / And it was exhausting! / I fed you meals, and you could've had your casts off two weeks ago! / That is not true. / It's not true? / So you're calling Dr. Harris a liar?
jokes.setup: Ann has confronted Andy about faking his recovery.
jokes.punchline: Andy's flat denial ('That is not true') followed by Ann's logical trap ('So you're calling Dr. Harris a liar?') is a perfect cringe comedy escalation.
jokes.explanation: Ann's 'so you're calling Dr. Harris a liar?' is a sharp logical trap that Andy cannot escape. The escalation toward the inevitable confrontation is well-paced.

jokes.text: Could I have gotten my casts off two weeks ago? Technically, yes. But... I really, really like it when you serve me food.
jokes.setup: Ann has cornered Andy into admitting the truth about his recovery.
jokes.punchline: Andy's confession — the great reveal of his motive — is 'I really, really like it when you serve me food.' The complete simplicity and honesty of this confession, delivered without apparent shame, is the perfect Andy moment.
jokes.explanation: This is the comedic peak of the episode and one of the best character jokes in the series. The entire Andy subplot — the faked recovery, the hand-and-foot service, Ann's band name suggestions — all collapses into this single confession. 'Technically, yes. But...' sets up maximum expectation for a dramatic reveal, and 'I really, really like it when you serve me food' is the most deflating and character-perfect answer possible. The 'really, really' is essential — it conveys genuine, unashamed sincerity. Perfect character integration, perfect economy, the most earned moment in the episode.

jokes.text: Get out. Get out of my house. / But what... / Take a walk with your overly-healed legs, and let me think about this relationship.
jokes.setup: Andy has just confessed he faked his recovery because he liked being served food.
jokes.punchline: 'Take a walk with your overly-healed legs' is a brilliantly specific eviction — the leg detail makes it not just anger but character-specific anger tied directly to the joke.
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'overly-healed legs' is exceptional comedy writing — it takes a specific narrative detail and weaponizes it as an insult. 'Overly-healed' is not standard English, and that freshness combined with its precision makes it hilarious. The callback structure is airtight: the setup is the entire episode's Andy subplot, and this is the perfect verbal payoff. Among the episode's very best lines.

jokes.text: Okay, this pit. Give it to me straight. Are we ever gonna turn it into a park? / Leslie, this is already a park! Look, I mean, you got Dirt Slide over here, you got Ring Around The Diaper you could play there, you've got Duck, Duck, Glass you could play right there. Mystery Trash. What's not to love about this park, right here, now?
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Mark seriously if the pit will ever become a park.
jokes.punchline: Mark's ironic naming of the pit's existing 'amenities' — Dirt Slide, Ring Around the Diaper, Duck Duck Glass, Mystery Trash — as though they're features of a functional park is a perfect absurdist riff.
jokes.explanation: This is a fantastic piece of joke writing. Each name is a perfect dark-absurdist riff on a classic park game: 'Ring Around the Diaper' (Ring Around the Rosy + diaper = baby waste contamination), 'Duck, Duck, Glass' (Duck, Duck, Goose + broken glass = injury hazard), 'Dirt Slide' (simplest possible name for a dangerous slide), 'Mystery Trash' (unknown refuse as a feature). The escalation works perfectly, and the ironic framing ('What's not to love?') caps it well. Among the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: I wish we could turn it into a pit, frankly, don't you?
jokes.setup: Mark has been ironically naming the pit's park features; now he continues the riff.
jokes.punchline: The suggestion that the ideal outcome would be turning the existing pit INTO a pit (i.e., it's already so bad that a pit would be an improvement) is a perfect logical paradox delivered deadpan.
jokes.explanation: The logical recursion — the pit is so bad we should turn it into a pit — is a great deadpan joke. The economy is perfect (11 words) and it extends the park names riff with an elegant capper.

jokes.text: Screw it. I'm gonna try to do it anyway. I mean, Kennedy put a man on the moon. He did. I can build one park.
jokes.setup: Mark has given Leslie an honest assessment: endless red tape, roadblocks, people who want her to fail.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's inspirational response escalates from a municipal parks project to the Apollo program with complete sincerity and zero awareness of the scale difference.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Leslie Knope moment — her ability to escalate a neighborhood park to the moon landing as equivalent achievements is both funny and endearing. The 'He did.' confirmation of the Kennedy fact to herself is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Hey, babe! Baby, open up! That guy Mark just fell in the pit! You know that guy Mark? Yeah. He just fell in the pit! You gotta go check it out. You're a nurse. I think he'd probably be hurt.
jokes.setup: Mark has just fallen in the pit. Andy knocks on Ann's door to tell her.
jokes.punchline: Andy uses Mark's injury as an excuse to re-engage with Ann — who just kicked him out — by appealing to her professional duty as a nurse. The 'I think he'd probably be hurt' is a masterpiece of Andy understatement.
jokes.explanation: 'I think he'd probably be hurt' after someone has fallen into a large pit is a perfect deadpan understatement from Andy. But the deeper joke is that Andy — who was just kicked out — has immediately found an angle to get Ann to come outside. It reveals character while being genuinely funny. Very strong character integration.

jokes.text: The episode ends with Andy's 'The Pit' song playing over Mark being carried out of the pit on a stretcher
jokes.setup: Andy wrote a song called 'The Pit' about falling in the pit. Mark has just fallen in the pit.
jokes.punchline: The song 'The Pit' playing as a diegetic/non-diegetic coda over Mark's rescue is the perfect circular structural joke — the song that 'informs people about a small public works project' is now directly relevant.
jokes.explanation: The use of 'The Pit' as the closing musical joke is an extremely well-earned structural callback that ties together multiple threads: Andy's song, the pit as the show's central McGuffin, Mark's fall, and Ann's description that the song 'informs people about a small public works project.' This is sophisticated comedy construction for a first season.

jokes.text: The episode closes on a reprise of The Pit Song as Ann reluctantly goes to help
jokes.setup: Mark has fallen in the pit; Ann is going to help
jokes.punchline: The Pit Song plays over the ending — 'Pit! I fell in it, the pit / We all fell in it, the pit' — now recontextualized as a literal description of what just happened to Mark
jokes.explanation: Masterful structural comedy — the Pit Song's 'We all fell in it, the pit' is now literally true. Andy's absurd song about the public works project becomes the episode's thematic punchline. The song's lyrics predicted/described the episode's final physical comedy beat. This kind of structural payoff is the best writing in the episode — it recontextualizes the earlier song as accidentally prophetic.

tmdb_overview: Leslie attends what she believes is a business meeting with an elderly local government bigwig, unaware that her mother has secretly set her up on a blind date. Andy plays his first gig since breaking both of his legs in the pit.
insight: Early season finds its footing: character comedy and cringe sustain a thin plot.
